\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The multiverse and its modal logic}

Forcing produces, from a universe $V$ of sets and a partial order of conditions, an extension
$V[G]$ containing a new generic object $G$. Iterating generates a vast network of universes: the
\emph{set-theoretic multiverse}. Its natural language is modal: $\Box p$ abbreviates ``$p$ holds
in every forcing extension of the current universe'' and $\Diamond p$ abbreviates ``$p$ holds in
some forcing extension''. Three structural properties of forcing give immediate lower bounds on
the valid schemes:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item trivial forcing gives $\Box p \to p$ (axiom $T$; reflexivity);
\item an iteration of forcings is a forcing, giving $\Box p \to \Box \Box p$ (axiom $4$;
transitivity);
\item two forcing extensions embed into a common extension, obtained by forcing with the
product, giving $\Diamond \Box p \to \Box \Diamond p$ (axiom $.2$; directedness).
\end{enumerate}
With the normal base logic $K$ this is the system $\mathsf{S4.2}$. Upper bounds require
\emph{control}. A \emph{button} is an assertion $p$ with $p \to \Box p$ valid at every world
(once true, permanently true); a \emph{switch} is an assertion with
$\Box(\Diamond p \wedge \Diamond \neg p)$ valid (its value can always be toggled either way).
The Continuum Hypothesis is the archetypal switch; assertions recording that some object has
irreversibly ceased to be definable are archetypal buttons.

\subsection{The gap closed here}

An abstract treatment may \emph{postulate} a reflexive, transitive, directed frame carrying
buttons and switches. A postulate is not a construction. The obligation is concrete: exhibit one
satisfaction relation, arising from an honest Boolean-valued construction, for which every frame
law, the button law, the switch law and both Continuum-Hypothesis branch conditions are
\emph{theorems}. This paper discharges that obligation at the propositional level and uses the
resulting object to settle several adjacent questions exactly. All results below are proved
outright, with no unproved set-theoretic hypotheses.

\section{Layer A: Boolean-valued semantics and generic quotients}

\subsection{Syntax and Boolean values}

Fix a set $\mathcal{A}$ of atoms. The language $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})$ is generated by
\[
p ::= a \mid \bot \mid p \to q \qquad (a \in \mathcal{A}),
\]
a functionally complete signature for classical logic. We abbreviate $\neg p := (p \to \bot)$,
$\top := \neg\bot$, $p \vee q := (\neg p \to q)$ and $p \wedge q := \neg(p \to \neg q)$.

Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra with Heyting implication $a \Rightarrow b := a^{\complement} \vee b$;
recall $a \wedge (a \Rightarrow b) \le b$ and the residuation law
$c \le a \Rightarrow b \iff c \wedge a \le b$.

\begin{definition}[Boolean value]
Given an assignment $v : \mathcal{A} \to B$, define $\bval{\cdot}_v$ recursively by
\[
\bval{a}_v = v(a), \qquad \bval{\bot}_v = \bot, \qquad
\bval{p \to q}_v = \bval{p}_v \Rightarrow \bval{q}_v .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Defined connectives]
$\bval{\neg p}_v = \bval{p}_v^{\complement}$, $\bval{\top}_v = \top$,
$\bval{p \vee q}_v = \bval{p}_v \vee \bval{q}_v$ and
$\bval{p \wedge q}_v = \bval{p}_v \wedge \bval{q}_v$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from $a \Rightarrow \bot = a^{\complement}$, $a \Rightarrow b = a^{\complement} \vee b$,
De Morgan and $\bot^{\complement} = \top$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Forcing closure}

Let $\vdash$ denote derivability in the Hilbert calculus with the schemes
\[
\text{(A1)}\ p \to (q \to p), \qquad
\text{(A2)}\ \bigl(p \to (q \to r)\bigr) \to \bigl((p \to q) \to (p \to r)\bigr), \qquad
\text{(A3)}\ \neg\neg p \to p,
\]
closed under modus ponens; this calculus is complete for classical propositional logic.

\begin{lemma}[Boolean forms of the axioms]\label{lem:hilbert}
In any Boolean algebra,
\[
a \Rightarrow (b \Rightarrow a) = \top, \qquad
\bigl(a \Rightarrow (b \Rightarrow c)\bigr) \Rightarrow
\bigl((a \Rightarrow b) \Rightarrow (a \Rightarrow c)\bigr) = \top, \qquad
a^{\complement\complement} \Rightarrow a = \top .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Strip the implications by residuation. The first becomes $\top \wedge a \wedge b \le a$. The
second becomes
$\top \wedge (a \Rightarrow (b \Rightarrow c)) \wedge (a \Rightarrow b) \wedge a \le c$,
whose left side is below
$\bigl((a \Rightarrow (b \Rightarrow c)) \wedge a\bigr) \wedge \bigl((a \Rightarrow b) \wedge
a\bigr) \le (b \Rightarrow c) \wedge b \le c$. The third is $a^{\complement\complement} = a$
with $a \Rightarrow a = \top$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forcing closure]\label{thm:closure}
If $\vdash p$ then $\bval{p}_v = \top$, for every Boolean algebra and every assignment.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the derivation. The axiom cases are Lemma~\ref{lem:hilbert}. For modus ponens, if
$\bval{p \to q}_v = \top$ and $\bval{p}_v = \top$ then
$\top = \bval{p}_v \wedge (\bval{p}_v \Rightarrow \bval{q}_v) \le \bval{q}_v$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Generic filters and the truth lemma}

\begin{definition}[Generic filter]
A \emph{generic filter} on $B$ is $U \subseteq B$ with: $\top \in U$; $\bot \notin U$; $U$
upward closed; $U$ closed under meets; and for every $a$, either $a \in U$ or
$a^{\complement} \in U$. Equivalently, $U$ is an ultrafilter.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:filter}
For a generic filter $U$: (i) $a^{\complement} \in U \iff a \notin U$; (ii)
$(a \Rightarrow b) \in U \iff (a \in U \Rightarrow b \in U)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) If both $a, a^{\complement} \in U$ then $\bot \in U$; conversely use decisiveness. (ii) If
$a \Rightarrow b \in U$ and $a \in U$ then $a \wedge (a \Rightarrow b) \in U$ and this is
$\le b$. Conversely: if $a \in U$ then $b \in U$ and $b \le a \Rightarrow b$; if $a \notin U$
then $a^{\complement} \in U$ and $a^{\complement} \le a \Rightarrow b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Generic quotient]
For $w : \mathcal{A} \to \{\text{true},\text{false}\}$ let $w \models p$ be the usual two-valued
satisfaction. The \emph{generic quotient} of $(B,v)$ by a generic filter $U$ is the two-valued
world $\quotient(v,U)(a) := (v(a) \in U)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Truth lemma]\label{thm:truth}
For every assertion $p$, $\quotient(v,U) \models p \iff \bval{p}_v \in U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $p$. Atoms hold by definition; $\bot$ by properness; the implication case is
Lemma~\ref{lem:filter}(ii).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Forcing]
A condition $b \in B$ \emph{forces} $p$, written $b \Vdash_v p$, when $b \le \bval{p}_v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
Forcing is monotone in the condition and closed under modus ponens; and if $b \in U$ and
$b \Vdash_v p$ then $\quotient(v,U) \models p$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Monotonicity is transitivity of $\le$; modus ponens follows from
$b \le \bval{p} \wedge (\bval{p} \Rightarrow \bval{q}) \le \bval{q}$; the last claim uses upward
closure and Theorem~\ref{thm:truth}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Branching}

Call $B$ \emph{rich} if every $b \neq \bot$ belongs to some generic filter.

\begin{theorem}[Branching theorem]\label{thm:branch}
Let $B$ be rich and $\bval{p}_v \notin \{\bot,\top\}$. Then there are generic filters $U,V$ with
$\quotient(v,U) \models p$ and $\quotient(v,V) \not\models p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Richness applied to $\bval{p}_v \ne \bot$ gives $U$; Theorem~\ref{thm:truth} gives truth.
Richness applied to $\bval{p}_v^{\complement} \ne \bot$ (equivalent to $\bval{p}_v \ne \top$)
gives $V$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:filter}(i) gives falsity.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Powerset algebras are rich, choice-freely]\label{prop:rich}
For any set $\Omega$ the principal filter $U_x = \{ s \subseteq \Omega : x \in s\}$ is generic,
and every nonempty $b \subseteq \Omega$ contains a point; hence $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ is rich.
\end{proposition}

\section{Layer B: the control frame of buttons and switches}

\begin{definition}[Control frame]
A \emph{control world} is a pair $w = (S,g)$ with $S$ a finite set of pushed buttons and
$g : \Sw \to \{0,1\}$ a switch setting. Accessibility is
$(S,g) \sqsubseteq (T,h) :\iff S \subseteq T$: an extension may push further buttons and reset
switches arbitrarily, but never unpush a button. For a predicate $P$,
$(\Box P)(w) :\iff \forall v (w \sqsubseteq v \to P(v))$ and
$(\Diamond P)(w) :\iff \exists v (w \sqsubseteq v \wedge P(v))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Frame laws]\label{prop:frame}
$\sqsubseteq$ is reflexive and transitive, and directed: for all $v_1,v_2$ there is $u$ with
$v_1 \sqsubseteq u$ and $v_2 \sqsubseteq u$, namely $u = (S_1 \cup S_2, g_1)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[$\mathsf{S4.2}$ soundness]\label{prop:s42frame}
For all predicates $P,Q$ and worlds $w$ the schemes $\Box P \to P$, $\Box P \to \Box\Box P$,
$\Box(P \to Q) \to (\Box P \to \Box Q)$ and $\Diamond \Box P \to \Box \Diamond P$ hold.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The first three use reflexivity, transitivity and pointwise reasoning. For $.2$: let $v$ witness
$\Diamond \Box P(w)$ and let $w \sqsubseteq u$; directedness gives $t$ above $v$ and $u$, and
$P(t)$ holds, so $\Diamond P(u)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
A predicate $P$ is a \emph{button} for $R$ if $R\,w\,v$ and $P(w)$ imply $P(v)$; it is a
\emph{switch} if $\Diamond P$ and $\Diamond \neg P$ hold at every world.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$\pushed_b(S,g) :\iff b \in S$ is a button; $\mathrm{on}_s(S,g) :\iff g(s) = 1$ is a switch, and
persistently so: $\Box(\Diamond\,\mathrm{on}_s \wedge \Diamond\neg\,\mathrm{on}_s)$ holds
everywhere.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Failure of $5$ and of Brouwer]\label{prop:five}
Let $b$ be a button and $P(v) :\iff b \notin v_1$. At $w = (\varnothing,g)$ we have $P(w)$, hence
$\Diamond P(w)$, but $\Box \Diamond P(w)$ fails, since no world above $(\{b\},g)$ satisfies $P$.
Hence both $\Diamond P \to \Box\Diamond P$ (axiom $5$) and $P \to \Box \Diamond P$ (axiom
$\mathrm{B}$) fail.
\end{proposition}

\section{Layer C: the realization}

\begin{definition}[Generic objects and stage assignments]
Let $\Gsp := \{0,1\}^{\Sw}$ be the space of generic objects and $B := \mathcal{P}(\Gsp)$. Atoms
are button atoms $\mathrm{btn}(b)$ and switch atoms $\mathrm{sw}(s)$. The stage-$S$ assignment is
\[
v_S(\mathrm{btn}(b)) := \begin{cases} \Gsp & b \in S,\\ \varnothing & b \notin S,\end{cases}
\qquad
v_S(\mathrm{sw}(s)) := \{ g \in \Gsp : g(s) = 1\},
\]
and we write $\bval{p}_S := \bval{p}_{v_S}$. Two-valued truth $(S,g) \models p$ is satisfaction
for the atomic diagram $\mathrm{btn}(b) \mapsto (b \in S)$, $\mathrm{sw}(s) \mapsto (g(s)=1)$.
\end{definition}

Button atoms receive only the extreme values $\bot,\top$; switch atoms receive genuinely
intermediate values, and this is the source of branching.

\begin{theorem}[Realization theorem]\label{thm:real}
For every stage $S$, every $g \in \Gsp$ and every assertion $p$,
\[
(S,g) \models p \quad\iff\quad g \in \bval{p}_S .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $U_g$ be the principal generic filter at $g$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:rich}). On atoms,
$\quotient(v_S,U_g)$ is exactly the atomic diagram of $(S,g)$: $g \in v_S(\mathrm{btn}(b))$ iff
$b \in S$, and $g \in v_S(\mathrm{sw}(s))$ iff $g(s) = 1$. Since satisfaction depends only on the
atomic diagram, $(S,g) \models p$ iff $\quotient(v_S,U_g) \models p$, which by
Theorem~\ref{thm:truth} is $\bval{p}_S \in U_g$, i.e.\ $g \in \bval{p}_S$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Buttons, derived}

\begin{definition}
$\mathrm{Pos}$ is the least class containing $\top$ and every button atom and closed under
$\wedge$ and $\vee$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pos}
For $p \in \mathrm{Pos}$: (i) $\bval{p}_S \in \{\varnothing, \Gsp\}$; (ii) $S \subseteq T$
implies $\bval{p}_S \subseteq \bval{p}_T$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Buttons are derived, not assumed]\label{thm:button}
Every $p \in \mathrm{Pos}$ defines a button: if $(S,g) \models p$ and $S \subseteq T$ then
$(T,h) \models p$ for every $h$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:real}, $g \in \bval{p}_S$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:pos}(i) also
$h \in \bval{p}_S$; by (ii) $h \in \bval{p}_T$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:real} again
$(T,h) \models p$.
\end{proof}

On the algebra side directedness has a counterpart: for a button atom,
$v_{S \cup T}(\mathrm{btn}(b)) = v_S(\mathrm{btn}(b)) \cup v_T(\mathrm{btn}(b))$.

\subsection{The Continuum-Hypothesis branches, derived}

Designate a switch $s_{\CH}$ and let $\CH$ abbreviate $\mathrm{sw}(s_{\CH})$.

\begin{lemma}
$\bval{\CH}_S \ne \varnothing$ and $\bval{\CH}_S \ne \Gsp$ for every stage $S$: the all-ones
generic object lies in the value, the all-zeros one does not.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Derived opposite CH branches]\label{thm:chbranch}
There are generic filters $U,V$ with $\quotient(v_S,U) \models \CH$ and
$\quotient(v_S,V) \not\models \CH$. Moreover, in the frame, both $\Diamond \CH$ and
$\Diamond \neg \CH$ hold at every world, witnessed by $(S,\mathbf{1})$ and $(S,\mathbf{0})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Packaged realization]\label{thm:package}
There is a single satisfaction relation --- the Boolean-valued one of Theorem~\ref{thm:real} ---
for which all of the following hold simultaneously: $\sqsubseteq$ is reflexive; transitive;
directed; every button atom defines a button; the designated CH atom defines a switch; and truth
at $(S,g)$ equals membership of $g$ in the stage-$S$ Boolean value.
\end{theorem}

\section{Exact calibration of the frame}

\begin{theorem}[$.2$ is exactly directedness]\label{thm:dot2}
Let $R$ be a relation on $W$ such that $\Diamond_R \Box_R P(w) \to \Box_R \Diamond_R P(w)$ for
every predicate $P$ and world $w$. Then $R$ is directed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the schema at $x$ to $P(t) :\iff R\,y\,t$. Then $\Diamond\Box P(x)$ holds, witnessed by
$y$; hence $\Box \Diamond P(x)$, and instantiating at $z$ yields $u$ with $R\,z\,u$ and
$R\,y\,u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One button refutes $\mathsf{S5}$]\label{thm:eucl}
The control frame is Euclidean --- the frame condition for axiom $5$ --- if and only if there
are no buttons.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $b$ is a button, then from $(\varnothing,\mathbf 0)$ both $(\{b\},\mathbf 0)$ and
$(\varnothing,\mathbf 0)$ are accessible, so Euclideanness would give $\{b\} \subseteq
\varnothing$. Conversely, with no buttons all worlds are mutually accessible.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two independent buttons refute linearity]\label{thm:dot3}
For $b_1 \ne b_2$ the schema
$\Box(\Box\,\pushed_{b_1} \to \pushed_{b_2}) \vee \Box(\Box\,\pushed_{b_2} \to \pushed_{b_1})$
fails at $(\varnothing,g)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
At $(\{b_1\},g)$ we have $\Box\,\pushed_{b_1}$ while $\pushed_{b_2}$ fails, refuting the left
disjunct; the right disjunct fails symmetrically at $(\{b_2\},g)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Soundness and independence}

\begin{definition}
Modal formulas are generated by $p ::= a \mid \bot \mid p \to q \mid \Box p$, with
$\Diamond p := \neg\Box\neg p$, and interpreted by the usual Kripke clauses. The calculus
$\mathsf{S4.2}$ consists of (A1)--(A3) together with
$K : \Box(p \to q) \to (\Box p \to \Box q)$, $T : \Box p \to p$, $4 : \Box p \to \Box\Box p$ and
$.2 : \Diamond\Box p \to \Box\Diamond p$, closed under modus ponens and necessitation. A
\emph{directed preorder} is a reflexive, transitive, directed frame.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness]\label{thm:sound}
Every theorem of $\mathsf{S4.2}$ is true at every world of every directed preorder under every
valuation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on derivations; $T$ uses reflexivity, $4$ transitivity, and $.2$ directedness exactly
as in Proposition~\ref{prop:s42frame}. Modus ponens and necessitation preserve validity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Independence of $5$ and of $.3$]\label{thm:indep}
Neither $\Diamond p \to \Box\Diamond p$ nor $\Box(\Box p \to q) \vee \Box(\Box q \to p)$ is
derivable in $\mathsf{S4.2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The finite two-button, one-switch control frame is a directed preorder
(Proposition~\ref{prop:frame}), and refutes the first formula by
Proposition~\ref{prop:five} and the second by Theorem~\ref{thm:dot3}. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:sound}.
\end{proof}

\section{The multiverse-invariant fragment}

\begin{definition}
An assertion is \emph{button-free} if it is built from switch atoms and $\bot$ by implication.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance of the button-free fragment]\label{thm:bfinv}
If $p$ is button-free then $(S,g) \models p \iff (T,g) \models p$ for all stages $S,T$. Hence
$p$ is simultaneously a button for the switch-preserving extension relation and for the
switch-preserving ground relation, and if $p$ holds at one world it holds throughout the entire
switch fibre.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Invariant fragment theorem]\label{thm:frag}
For an arbitrary assertion $p$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $p$ is invariant along the button order: $(S,g)\models p \iff (T,g)\models p$ for all
$S,T,g$;
\item $p$ is equivalent, at every world, to a button-free assertion.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is Theorem~\ref{thm:bfinv}. For (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) let $p^{\bot}$ arise
from $p$ by substituting $\bot$ for each button atom. It is button-free, and an induction gives
the substitution lemma $(S,g)\models p^{\bot} \iff (\varnothing,g)\models p$ for every $S$.
Invariance identifies the right-hand side with $(S,g)\models p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness]
A bare button atom is not invariant: it is true at $(\{b\},g)$ and false at $(\varnothing,g)$.
\end{proposition}

\section{Calibrating branching by preserved backgrounds}

\begin{theorem}[Exact preservation criterion]\label{thm:bg}
Let $B$ be rich, $b \in B$ a background and $p$ an assertion. There exist generic filters $U,V$
with $b \in U$, $\quotient(v,U)\models p$, $b \in V$ and $\quotient(v,V)\not\models p$ if and
only if
\[
b \wedge \bval{p}_v \ne \bot \quad\text{and}\quad b \wedge \bval{p}_v^{\complement} \ne \bot .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) By Theorem~\ref{thm:truth}, $\bval{p}_v \in U$, so $b \wedge \bval{p}_v \in U$,
which is therefore not $\bot$; symmetrically for $V$ using
Lemma~\ref{lem:filter}(i). ($\Leftarrow$) Apply richness to the two nonzero meets and use upward
closure.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Button-definable backgrounds always branch]
If $b \in S$, the background $v_S(\mathrm{btn}(b)) = \Gsp$ meets both $\bval{\CH}_S$ and its
complement, so it survives into a $\CH$ branch and a $\neg\CH$ branch of one and the same
Boolean-valued universe. Frame-side: for any property $\Theta$ of stages with $\Theta(S)$, the
worlds $(S,\mathbf 1)$ and $(S,\mathbf 0)$ are accessible from $(S,g)$, satisfy $\Theta$, and
disagree about $\CH$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preservation obstruction]
The switch-dependent background $b = \bval{\CH}_S$ satisfies $b \ne \bot$ but
$b \wedge \bval{\CH}_S^{\complement} = \bot$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:bg} no pair of opposite
branches preserves it.
\end{theorem}

\section{Ground/extension bimodality}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{ground} relation is $(S,g) \sqsupseteq_{\mathrm{gnd}} (T,h) :\iff T \subseteq S$, the
converse of $\sqsubseteq$, with modalities $\bgnd, \dgnd$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
The ground relation is reflexive, transitive and downward directed (two grounds of a world have
a common ground, the intersection of their pushed sets). The world $(\varnothing,g)$ is a ground
of every world --- the analogue of the \emph{mantle} --- and $\dgnd(\text{no button pushed})$
holds everywhere.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Mixed tense validity and bimodal separation]\label{thm:bimodal}
For every predicate $P$ and world $w$, $P(w)$ implies $\Box\,\dgnd\,P(w)$; indeed $w$ is itself
a ground of each of its extensions. Yet on the same frame, with at least one button, the
unimodal Brouwer axiom $P \to \Box \Diamond P$ fails. Hence the ground modality contributes
validities the forcing modality alone cannot express.
\end{theorem}

\section{Bounded morphisms and transfer}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{bounded morphism} $f : (W,R) \to (W',R')$ satisfies \emph{forth}
($R\,w\,v \Rightarrow R'\,f(w)\,f(v)$) and \emph{back}
($R'\,f(w)\,u \Rightarrow \exists v\,(R\,w\,v \wedge f(v)=u)$). Bounded morphisms compose.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Truth and validity transfer]\label{thm:transfer}
For a bounded morphism $f$ and valuation $V'$ on $W'$, a modal formula holds at $w$ under
$V' \circ f$ iff it holds at $f(w)$ under $V'$. Consequently, if $f$ is surjective, every
formula valid on $(W,R)$ is valid on $(W',R')$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the formula; the $\Box$ case uses \emph{back} in one direction and \emph{forth} in
the other. Surjectivity transfers validity by pulling an arbitrary world back along $f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Switches are semantically free]
The projection $(S,g) \mapsto S$ is a surjective bounded morphism from the control frame onto
the pure button order; hence switches contribute no modal validities of their own.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Chains are bounded images; strict containment]\label{thm:chain}
The cardinality map $S \mapsto |S|$ is a surjective bounded morphism from the $n$-button order
onto the chain $\{0,\dots,n\}$. Consequently, for $n \ge 2$, the modal logic of the $n$-button
control frame is contained in the logic of the $(n+1)$-element chain, and strictly so:
linearity is valid on every total frame but is refuted on the control frame by two independent
buttons.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Back} for the cardinality map: given $|S| \le k \le n$, extend $S$ to a set of size exactly
$k$. Validity of linearity on total frames: if both disjuncts failed at $w$, we would obtain
successors $v$ (with $\Box p$, $\neg q$) and $u$ (with $\Box q$, $\neg p$), and comparability of
$v,u$ gives a contradiction either way. Failure on the control frame is
Theorem~\ref{thm:dot3}; containment is Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}.
\end{proof}

\section{Counting the finite frames}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:count}
For a finite set $s$, $\sum_{t \subseteq s} 2^{|t|} = 3^{|s|}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction: subsets of $s \cup \{a\}$ with $a \notin s$ split into those omitting $a$
(contributing $\sum_{t \subseteq s} 2^{|t|}$) and those containing it (contributing twice as
much), giving a factor $3$. Combinatorially, each element occupies one of three states.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact size of the forcing relation]\label{thm:size}
The control frame with $n$ buttons and $m$ switches has $2^{n+m}$ worlds and exactly
$3^n \cdot 4^m$ accessibility pairs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The worlds accessible to a fixed $(T,h)$ form $\mathcal{P}(T) \times \{0,1\}^{\Sw}$, of size
$2^{|T|} 2^m$. Summing over all $T$ and all $h$ gives
$\sum_{T} 2^{|T|} \cdot 4^m = 3^n 4^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:count}.
\end{proof}

Each button admits three states across an accessible pair (off/off, off/on, on/on --- never
on/off); each switch admits four. The formula is the arithmetical signature of irreversibility
versus freedom.

\section{Algorithms}

The finite frames are small enough to compute with. Representing $\mathcal{P}(\Gsp)$ with
$|\Gsp| = 2^m$ as bitmasks of width $2^m$, the Boolean value $\bval{p}_S$ is computed by
structural recursion in $O(|p|)$ bitwise operations, and Theorem~\ref{thm:real} reduces
two-valued evaluation at $(S,g)$ to a single bit test. Enumerating the $2^{n+m}$ worlds and
testing $S \subseteq T$ pairwise confirms the closed form of Theorem~\ref{thm:size} in
$O(4^{n+m})$ bit operations. Schematic modal validity on a finite frame is decided by
quantifying over the $2^{|W|}$ predicates per schematic letter --- exponential, but immediate
for the frames producing the canonical countermodels. Invariance is decided in
$O(|p| \cdot 2^{n+m})$ by comparing $p$ with its button-free normal form $p^{\bot}$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:frag}), and two-sided branch preservation is decided by two word operations
via Theorem~\ref{thm:bg}.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Derived rather than assumed}

Directedness comes from the union of stages; the button law comes from monotonicity of Boolean
values along the stage order transported by the realization theorem; CH branching comes from the
branching theorem applied to a value provably distinct from $\bot$ and $\top$; forcing closure
comes from soundness of Boolean-valued semantics for a complete Hilbert calculus. All of these
are packaged as a single satisfaction relation validating them at once
(Theorem~\ref{thm:package}).

\subsection{Scope and limitations}

The construction is propositional: atoms stand for set-theoretic assertions and their modal
interplay is faithful, but the quantifier structure of genuine set-theoretic sentences is not
modelled. The algebra is a powerset algebra, hence complete and atomic, whereas genuine forcing
algebras are typically atomless; genericity here is decisiveness of the filter rather than
meeting all dense sets of a ground model. What survives, and is all the modal analysis requires,
is the truth lemma, forcing closure and branching. Finally, buttons and switches are stipulated
as atoms of the corresponding kinds; what is \emph{derived} is that they behave as buttons and
switches in the realized semantics, and that the positive fragment generated by button atoms
obeys the button law.

\subsection{Multiverse truth versus forcing necessity}

$\Box p$ says $p$ survives all extensions; it says nothing about grounds, hence nothing about
truth throughout the multiverse. Theorem~\ref{thm:frag} shows that genuine invariance is
bidirectional and is a real restriction --- exactly the assertions never mentioning a button ---
and Theorem~\ref{thm:bimodal} shows that admitting the ground modality creates new validities.

\section{Future work}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item \textbf{Finite-frame completeness of $\mathsf{S4.2}$.} Conjecture: a modal formula is
derivable in $\mathsf{S4.2}$ iff it is valid on every finite button--switch control frame.
Soundness is Theorem~\ref{thm:sound} and the hardest refuting instances are
Theorem~\ref{thm:indep}; what remains is a filtration argument turning an arbitrary finite
directed-preorder countermodel into a button--switch product. Theorem~\ref{thm:size} quantifies
the available room and Theorem~\ref{thm:chain} shows the technique works in special cases.
\item \textbf{A Boolean-valued Lindenbaum theorem.} Characterize the algebras arising as value
algebras of realizations with prescribed richness and branching data.
\item \textbf{Beyond the propositional level.} Add Boolean-valued quantifier clauses
$\bval{\forall x\,\varphi} = \bigwedge_a \bval{\varphi(a)}$, requiring completeness of the
algebra, and determine which results survive.
\item \textbf{Large-cardinal calibration.} Parameterize backgrounds by invariants the forcing
must preserve, aiming at a uniform preparation principle producing both branches while
preserving a fixed hierarchy of indestructible assertions.
\item \textbf{The full bimodal logic.} Axiomatize the interaction logic generated by upward
directedness, downward directedness and a least ground.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

Abstract accounts of the forcing multiverse specify the interface a semantics must satisfy: a
reflexive, transitive, directed frame with buttons and switches. This paper supplies a semantics
meeting that interface exactly, built from Boolean values and generic quotients, in which the
interface conditions are theorems. Around it the modal picture becomes exact: $.2$ is
directedness, $5$ is the absence of buttons, linearity fails for two independent buttons,
invariance is button-freeness, two-sided branch preservation is a Boolean meet condition,
switches are semantically free, and the accessibility relation of the $n$-button, $m$-switch
frame has exactly $3^n 4^m$ pairs. The control panel of irreversible buttons and free switches
is not a metaphor for forcing; it is a generic quotient of a Boolean-valued universe.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Syntax:  p ::= atom | ⊥ | p → q,  with atoms ("btn", i) and ("sw", j)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Atom = Tuple[str, int]
Formula = Tuple  # ("atom", Atom) | ("fls",) | ("imp", Formula, Formula)

FLS: Formula = ("fls",)


def atom(kind: str, index: int) -> Formula:
    """Atomic assertion: kind is 'btn' (a button) or 'sw' (a switch)."""
    return ("atom", (kind, index))


def imp(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Material implication p → q."""
    return ("imp", p, q)


def neg(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Negation ¬p := p → ⊥."""
    return imp(p, FLS)


TRU: Formula = neg(FLS)


def disj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Disjunction p ∨ q := ¬p → q."""
    return imp(neg(p), q)


def conj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Conjunction p ∧ q := ¬(p → ¬q)."""
    return neg(imp(p, neg(q)))


def show(p: Formula) -> str:
    """Human-readable rendering of a formula."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return "⊥"
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return ("b%d" % i) if kind == "btn" else ("s%d" % i)
    left, right = p[1], p[2]
    if right == FLS:
        return "¬" + show(left)
    return "(%s → %s)" % (show(left), show(right))


def atoms_of(p: Formula) -> List[Atom]:
    """All atoms occurring in p, without repetition, in order of appearance."""
    out: List[Atom] = []

    def walk(q: Formula) -> None:
        if q[0] == "atom":
            if q[1] not in out:
                out.append(q[1])
        elif q[0] == "imp":
            walk(q[1])
            walk(q[2])

    walk(p)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Layer A: Boolean values over the powerset algebra of generic objects
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def top_mask(m: int) -> int:
    """The element ⊤ of the algebra P({0,1}^m), as a bitmask of width 2^m."""
    return (1 << (1 << m)) - 1


def generic_objects(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All 2^m switch settings, indexed consistently with the bitmask order."""
    return [tuple(reversed(bits)) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def generic_index(g: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Index of the generic object g in the enumeration `generic_objects`."""
    return sum(bit << k for k, bit in enumerate(g))


def make_assignment(stage: FrozenSet[int], n: int, m: int) -> Dict[Atom, int]:
    """Stage-`stage` assignment of Boolean values to all atoms."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    assign: Dict[Atom, int] = {}
    for i in range(n):
        assign[("btn", i)] = full if i in stage else 0
    for j in range(m):
        mask = 0
        for idx, g in enumerate(generic_objects(m)):
            if g[j] == 1:
                mask |= 1 << idx
        assign[("sw", j)] = mask
    return assign


def bval(p: Formula, assign: Dict[Atom, int], m: int) -> int:
    """Boolean value ⟦p⟧ ∈ P({0,1}^m), computed by structural recursion."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return 0
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return assign[p[1]]
    a = bval(p[1], assign, m)
    b = bval(p[2], assign, m)
    return (full & ~a) | b  # a ⇒ b = aᶜ ∨ b


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Two-valued satisfaction at a control world
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

World = Tuple[FrozenSet[int], Tuple[int, ...]]


def csat(w: World, p: Formula) -> bool:
    """Two-valued truth of p at the control world w = (S, g)."""
    stage, g = w
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return False
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return (i in stage) if kind == "btn" else (g[i] == 1)
    return (not csat(w, p[1])) or csat(w, p[2])


def worlds(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    """All 2^(n+m) control worlds with n buttons and m switches."""
    out: List[World] = []
    for r in range(n + 1):
        for combo in combinations(range(n), r):
            for g in generic_objects(m):
                out.append((frozenset(combo), g))
    return out


def accessible(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Forcing accessibility: buttons may only be pushed, never unpushed."""
    return w[0] <= v[0]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Modal operators on predicates over a finite frame
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Pred = Callable[[World], bool]


def box(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def dia(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def gbox(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    """Ground necessity: quantify over worlds of which w is an extension."""
    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def gdia(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    """Ground possibility."""
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def all_predicates(ws: Sequence[World]) -> Iterable[Pred]:
    """All 2^|W| predicates on a finite frame (used for schematic validity)."""
    k = len(ws)
    index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(ws)}
    for mask in range(1 << k):
        yield (lambda mask=mask: (lambda w: bool(mask >> index[w] & 1)))()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 1 -- forcing closure: tautologies have Boolean value ⊤
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_forcing_closure(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. FORCING CLOSURE:  every classical tautology has Boolean value ⊤")
    print("=" * 74)
    p, q, r = atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)
    axioms = {
        "A1  p → (q → p)": imp(p, imp(q, p)),
        "A2  (p→(q→r)) → ((p→q)→(p→r))": imp(
            imp(p, imp(q, r)), imp(imp(p, q), imp(p, r))
        ),
        "A3  ¬¬p → p": imp(neg(neg(p)), p),
        "excluded middle  p ∨ ¬p": disj(p, neg(p)),
        "Peirce  ((p→q)→p)→p": imp(imp(imp(p, q), p), p),
    }
    full = top_mask(m)
    for stage in (frozenset(), frozenset({0}), frozenset({0, 1})):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
        for name, f in axioms.items():
            value = bval(f, assign, m)
            assert value == full, (name, stage, value)
    print("   all axioms and tautologies evaluate to ⊤ = %s at every stage" % bin(full))
    # a non-theorem does not:
    contingent = atom("sw", 0)
    assign = make_assignment(frozenset(), n, m)
    print("   by contrast ⟦s0⟧ = %s  (neither ⊥ nor ⊤)" % bin(bval(contingent, assign, m)))
    print()

def demo_truth_lemma(n: int = 2, m: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)

    print("=" * 74)
    formulas = _sample_formulas(n, m)
    checked = 0
    for stage in _stages(n):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)

def demo_realization(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. REALIZATION THEOREM:  (S,g) ⊨ p   iff   g ∈ ⟦p⟧_S")

def demo_frame_logic(n: int = 2, m: int = 1) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. FRAME LAWS, S4.2 SOUNDNESS, AND THE FAILURE OF 5, B AND .3")
    print("=" * 74)
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    assert all(accessible(w, w) for w in ws)
    assert all(
        accessible(w, u)
        for w, v, u in product(ws, ws, ws)
        if accessible(w, v) and accessible(v, u)
    )
    directed = all(
        any(accessible(v1, u) and accessible(v2, u) for u in ws)
        for v1, v2 in product(ws, ws)
    )
    print("   reflexive: yes    transitive: yes    directed: %s" % directed)

    ok_T = ok_4 = ok_dot2 = True
    for P in all_predicates(ws):
        for w in ws:
            ok_T &= (not box(ws, P)(w)) or P(w)
            ok_4 &= (not box(ws, P)(w)) or box(ws, box(ws, P))(w)
            ok_dot2 &= (not dia(ws, box(ws, P))(w)) or box(ws, dia(ws, P))(w)
    print("   T (□p→p): %s    4 (□p→□□p): %s    .2 (◇□p→□◇p): %s"
          % (ok_T, ok_4, ok_dot2))

    # axiom 5 and Brouwer fail for P = "button 0 is still unpushed"
    P_unpushed: Pred = lambda w: 0 not in w[0]
    w0: World = (frozenset(), generic_objects(m)[0])
    print("   counterexample predicate: 'button 0 unpushed', base world S=∅")
    print("      ◇P holds:            %s" % dia(ws, P_unpushed)(w0))
    print("      P holds:             %s" % P_unpushed(w0))
    print("      □◇P holds:           %s   ->  axiom 5 and Brouwer both FAIL"
          % box(ws, dia(ws, P_unpushed))(w0))

    # linearity .3 fails with two independent buttons
    P1: Pred = lambda w: 0 in w[0]
    P2: Pred = lambda w: 1 in w[0]
    left = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P1)(v)) or P2(v))(w0)
    right = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P2)(v)) or P1(v))(w0)
    print("      .3  □(□p→q) ∨ □(□q→p) at S=∅: %s ∨ %s = %s   ->  FAILS"
          % (left, right, left or right))

    # the mixed tense axiom p → □ ◇̌ p is valid on the same frame
    tense_ok = all(
        (not P(w)) or box(ws, gdia(ws, P))(w)
        for P in all_predicates(ws)
        for w in ws
    )
    print("   mixed tense axiom p → □◇̌p (ground modality): %s" % tense_ok)
    print("      => bimodal separation: □◇̌ valid while □◇ (Brouwer) fails")
    print()

def demo_buttons_and_branches(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. DERIVED BUTTONS AND DERIVED CH BRANCHES")
    print("=" * 74)
    positive = [
        atom("btn", 0),
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),
        conj(TRU, disj(atom("btn", 0), conj(atom("btn", 1), atom("btn", 0)))),
    ]
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    for f in positive:
        # Boolean-valued monotonicity along the stage order
        for S, T in product(_stages(n), _stages(n)):
            if S <= T:
                vs = bval(f, make_assignment(S, n, m), m)
                vt = bval(f, make_assignment(T, n, m), m)
                assert vs & ~vt == 0, (show(f), S, T)
        # the resulting button law in the frame
        assert all(
            (not csat(w, f)) or csat(v, f)
            for w, v in product(ws, ws)
            if accessible(w, v)
        )
        print("   %-42s is a button (monotone Boolean value)" % show(f))

    ch = atom("sw", 0)  # the designated CH switch
    for S in _stages(n):
        value = bval(ch, make_assignment(S, n, m), m)
        assert value != 0 and value != top_mask(m)
    print("   ⟦CH⟧_S is neither ⊥ nor ⊤ at every stage -> branching theorem applies")
    for w in ws:
        assert dia(ws, lambda v: csat(v, ch))(w)
        assert dia(ws, lambda v: not csat(v, ch))(w)
    print("   ◇CH ∧ ◇¬CH holds at every one of the %d worlds: CH is a switch" % len(ws))
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 6 -- the invariant fragment theorem
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def button_free_normal_form(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Substitute ⊥ for every button atom: the canonical button-free candidate."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return p
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return FLS if p[1][0] == "btn" else p
    return imp(button_free_normal_form(p[1]), button_free_normal_form(p[2]))


def is_invariant(p: Formula, n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """Does the truth value of p depend only on the switch setting?"""
    for g in generic_objects(m):
        values = {csat((S, g), p) for S in _stages(n)}
        if len(values) > 1:
            return False
    return True


def demo_invariant_fragment(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. INVARIANT FRAGMENT THEOREM:  invariance ⟺ button-free normal form")
    print("=" * 74)
    tests = [
        atom("sw", 0),
        imp(atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)),
        atom("btn", 0),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), neg(atom("btn", 0))),          # a tautology: invariant
        imp(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 0)),                # invariant
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0)),                # not invariant
    ]
    for p in tests:
        inv = is_invariant(p, n, m)
        nf = button_free_normal_form(p)

            for S in _stages(n)

def survives_both_branches(background: int, value: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥ -- necessary and sufficient."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    return (background & value) != 0 and (background & full & ~value) != 0


def demo_branch_preservation(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. BRANCH PRESERVATION:  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥")
    print("=" * 74)
    stage = frozenset({0})
    assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
    ch = atom("sw", 0)
    value = bval(ch, assign, m)
    cases = {
        "button background  ⟦b0⟧ (b0 pushed)": bval(atom("btn", 0), assign, m),
        "trivial background ⊤": top_mask(m),
        "switch background  ⟦s0⟧ = ⟦CH⟧": value,
        "opposite switch    ⟦¬s0⟧": bval(neg(ch), assign, m),
        "unpushed button    ⟦b1⟧": bval(atom("btn", 1), assign, m),
    }
    for name, b in cases.items():
        print("   %-38s  b=%-8s survives both CH branches: %s"
              % (name, bin(b), survives_both_branches(b, value, m)))
    print("   -> button-definable backgrounds branch; switch-entangled ones cannot,")
    print("      and an inconsistent background (⊥) branches vacuously nowhere.")
    print()

def count_accessibility_pairs(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of the pairs (w,v) with w ⊑ v."""
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    return sum(1 for w, v in product(ws, ws) if accessible(w, v))


def demo_counting(max_n: int = 3, max_m: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. EXACT SIZE OF THE FORCING RELATION:  |⊑| = 3^n · 4^m")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    n  m   worlds 2^(n+m)   brute force   3^n·4^m   match")
    for n in range(max_n + 1):
        for m in range(max_m + 1):
            if n + m > 5:
                continue
            brute = count_accessibility_pairs(n, m)
            closed = 3 ** n * 4 ** m
            assert brute == closed
            print("   %2d %2d   %12d   %11d   %7d   %s"
                  % (n, m, 2 ** (n + m), brute, closed, brute == closed))
    print("   three states per button (off/off, off/on, on/on -- never on/off),")
    print("   four per switch (its value before and after are unconstrained).")
    print()

def _stages(n: int) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """All 2^n stages (sets of pushed buttons)."""
    return [
        frozenset(c) for r in range(n + 1) for c in combinations(range(n), r)
    ]


def _sample_formulas(n: int, m: int) -> List[Formula]:
    """A spread of test formulas mixing button and switch atoms."""
    b0, b1 = atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", min(1, n - 1))
    s0, s1 = atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", min(1, m - 1))
    return [
        FLS,
        TRU,
        b0,
        s0,
        neg(b0),
        neg(s0),
        imp(b0, s0),
        conj(b0, s0),
        disj(b0, s0),
        conj(disj(b0, b1), neg(s1)),
        imp(conj(s0, s1), disj(b0, neg(b1))),
    ]

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Syntax:  p ::= atom | ⊥ | p → q,  with atoms ("btn", i) and ("sw", j)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Atom = Tuple[str, int]
Formula = Tuple  # ("atom", Atom) | ("fls",) | ("imp", Formula, Formula)

FLS: Formula = ("fls",)


def atom(kind: str, index: int) -> Formula:
    """Atomic assertion: kind is 'btn' (a button) or 'sw' (a switch)."""
    return ("atom", (kind, index))


def imp(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Material implication p → q."""
    return ("imp", p, q)


def neg(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Negation ¬p := p → ⊥."""
    return imp(p, FLS)


TRU: Formula = neg(FLS)


def disj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Disjunction p ∨ q := ¬p → q."""
    return imp(neg(p), q)


def conj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Conjunction p ∧ q := ¬(p → ¬q)."""
    return neg(imp(p, neg(q)))


def show(p: Formula) -> str:
    """Human-readable rendering of a formula."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return "⊥"
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return ("b%d" % i) if kind == "btn" else ("s%d" % i)
    left, right = p[1], p[2]
    if right == FLS:
        return "¬" + show(left)
    return "(%s → %s)" % (show(left), show(right))


def atoms_of(p: Formula) -> List[Atom]:
    """All atoms occurring in p, without repetition, in order of appearance."""
    out: List[Atom] = []

    def walk(q: Formula) -> None:
        if q[0] == "atom":
            if q[1] not in out:
                out.append(q[1])
        elif q[0] == "imp":
            walk(q[1])
            walk(q[2])

    walk(p)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Layer A: Boolean values over the powerset algebra of generic objects
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def top_mask(m: int) -> int:
    """The element ⊤ of the algebra P({0,1}^m), as a bitmask of width 2^m."""
    return (1 << (1 << m)) - 1


def generic_objects(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All 2^m switch settings, indexed consistently with the bitmask order."""
    return [tuple(reversed(bits)) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def generic_index(g: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Index of the generic object g in the enumeration `generic_objects`."""
    return sum(bit << k for k, bit in enumerate(g))


def make_assignment(stage: FrozenSet[int], n: int, m: int) -> Dict[Atom, int]:
    """Stage-`stage` assignment of Boolean values to all atoms."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    assign: Dict[Atom, int] = {}
    for i in range(n):
        assign[("btn", i)] = full if i in stage else 0
    for j in range(m):
        mask = 0
        for idx, g in enumerate(generic_objects(m)):
            if g[j] == 1:
                mask |= 1 << idx
        assign[("sw", j)] = mask
    return assign


def bval(p: Formula, assign: Dict[Atom, int], m: int) -> int:
    """Boolean value ⟦p⟧ ∈ P({0,1}^m), computed by structural recursion."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return 0
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return assign[p[1]]
    a = bval(p[1], assign, m)
    b = bval(p[2], assign, m)
    return (full & ~a) | b  # a ⇒ b = aᶜ ∨ b


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Two-valued satisfaction at a control world
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

World = Tuple[FrozenSet[int], Tuple[int, ...]]


def csat(w: World, p: Formula) -> bool:
    """Two-valued truth of p at the control world w = (S, g)."""
    stage, g = w
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return False
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return (i in stage) if kind == "btn" else (g[i] == 1)
    return (not csat(w, p[1])) or csat(w, p[2])


def worlds(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    """All 2^(n+m) control worlds with n buttons and m switches."""
    out: List[World] = []
    for r in range(n + 1):
        for combo in combinations(range(n), r):
            for g in generic_objects(m):
                out.append((frozenset(combo), g))
    return out


def accessible(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Forcing accessibility: buttons may only be pushed, never unpushed."""
    return w[0] <= v[0]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Modal operators on predicates over a finite frame
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Pred = Callable[[World], bool]


def box(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def dia(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def gbox(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    """Ground necessity: quantify over worlds of which w is an extension."""
    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def gdia(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    """Ground possibility."""
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def all_predicates(ws: Sequence[World]) -> Iterable[Pred]:
    """All 2^|W| predicates on a finite frame (used for schematic validity)."""
    k = len(ws)
    index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(ws)}
    for mask in range(1 << k):
        yield (lambda mask=mask: (lambda w: bool(mask >> index[w] & 1)))()

def demo_forcing_closure(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. FORCING CLOSURE:  every classical tautology has Boolean value ⊤")
    print("=" * 74)
    p, q, r = atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)
    axioms = {
        "A1  p → (q → p)": imp(p, imp(q, p)),
        "A2  (p→(q→r)) → ((p→q)→(p→r))": imp(
            imp(p, imp(q, r)), imp(imp(p, q), imp(p, r))
        ),

        "excluded middle  p ∨ ¬p": disj(p, neg(p)),

    full = top_mask(m)
    for stage in (frozenset(), frozenset({0}), frozenset({0, 1})):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)

            value = bval(f, assign, m)
            assert value == full, (name, stage, value)
    print("   all axioms and tautologies evaluate to ⊤ = %s at every stage" % bin(full))
    # a non-theorem does not:
    contingent = atom("sw", 0)
    assign = make_assignment(frozenset(), n, m)
    print("   by contrast ⟦s0⟧ = %s  (neither ⊥ nor ⊤)" % bin(bval(contingent, assign, m)))
    print()

def demo_truth_lemma(n: int = 2, m: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. TRUTH LEMMA:  quot(v,U_g) ⊨ p   iff   ⟦p⟧ ∈ U_g   (U_g principal at g)")
    print("=" * 74)
    formulas = _sample_formulas(n, m)
    checked = 0
    for stage in _stages(n):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)

def demo_frame_logic(n: int = 2, m: int = 1) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. FRAME LAWS, S4.2 SOUNDNESS, AND THE FAILURE OF 5, B AND .3")
    print("=" * 74)
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    assert all(accessible(w, w) for w in ws)
    assert all(
        accessible(w, u)
        for w, v, u in product(ws, ws, ws)
        if accessible(w, v) and accessible(v, u)
    )
    directed = all(
        any(accessible(v1, u) and accessible(v2, u) for u in ws)
        for v1, v2 in product(ws, ws)
    )
    print("   reflexive: yes    transitive: yes    directed: %s" % directed)

    ok_T = ok_4 = ok_dot2 = True
    for P in all_predicates(ws):
        for w in ws:
            ok_T &= (not box(ws, P)(w)) or P(w)
            ok_4 &= (not box(ws, P)(w)) or box(ws, box(ws, P))(w)
            ok_dot2 &= (not dia(ws, box(ws, P))(w)) or box(ws, dia(ws, P))(w)
    print("   T (□p→p): %s    4 (□p→□□p): %s    .2 (◇□p→□◇p): %s"
          % (ok_T, ok_4, ok_dot2))

    # axiom 5 and Brouwer fail for P = "button 0 is still unpushed"
    P_unpushed: Pred = lambda w: 0 not in w[0]
    w0: World = (frozenset(), generic_objects(m)[0])
    print("   counterexample predicate: 'button 0 unpushed', base world S=∅")
    print("      ◇P holds:            %s" % dia(ws, P_unpushed)(w0))
    print("      P holds:             %s" % P_unpushed(w0))
    print("      □◇P holds:           %s   ->  axiom 5 and Brouwer both FAIL"
          % box(ws, dia(ws, P_unpushed))(w0))

    # linearity .3 fails with two independent buttons
    P1: Pred = lambda w: 0 in w[0]
    P2: Pred = lambda w: 1 in w[0]
    left = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P1)(v)) or P2(v))(w0)
    right = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P2)(v)) or P1(v))(w0)
    print("      .3  □(□p→q) ∨ □(□q→p) at S=∅: %s ∨ %s = %s   ->  FAILS"
          % (left, right, left or right))

    # the mixed tense axiom p → □ ◇̌ p is valid on the same frame
    tense_ok = all(
        (not P(w)) or box(ws, gdia(ws, P))(w)
        for P in all_predicates(ws)
        for w in ws
    )
    print("   mixed tense axiom p → □◇̌p (ground modality): %s" % tense_ok)
    print("      => bimodal separation: □◇̌ valid while □◇ (Brouwer) fails")
    print()

    print("=" * 74)
    positive = [

        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),

#  Demo 6 -- the invariant fragment theorem
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def button_free_normal_form(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Substitute ⊥ for every button atom: the canonical button-free candidate."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return p
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return FLS if p[1][0] == "btn" else p
    return imp(button_free_normal_form(p[1]), button_free_normal_form(p[2]))


def is_invariant(p: Formula, n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """Does the truth value of p depend only on the switch setting?"""
    for g in generic_objects(m):
        values = {csat((S, g), p) for S in _stages(n)}
        if len(values) > 1:
            return False
    return True


def demo_invariant_fragment(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. INVARIANT FRAGMENT THEOREM:  invariance ⟺ button-free normal form")
    print("=" * 74)
    tests = [
        atom("sw", 0),
        imp(atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)),
        atom("btn", 0),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), neg(atom("btn", 0))),          # a tautology: invariant
        imp(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 0)),                # invariant
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0)),                # not invariant
    ]
    for p in tests:
        inv = is_invariant(p, n, m)
        nf = button_free_normal_form(p)
        agrees = all(
            csat((S, g), p) == csat((S, g), nf)
            for S in _stages(n)
            for g in generic_objects(m)
        )
        assert inv == agrees, show(p)
        print("   %-28s invariant=%-5s  normal form %-22s agrees=%s"
              % (show(p), inv, show(nf), agrees))
    print("   (equality of the two columns is exactly the fragment theorem)")
    print()

def survives_both_branches(background: int, value: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥ -- necessary and sufficient."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    return (background & value) != 0 and (background & full & ~value) != 0


def demo_branch_preservation(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. BRANCH PRESERVATION:  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥")
    print("=" * 74)

    assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
    ch = atom("sw", 0)
    value = bval(ch, assign, m)

    ws = worlds(n, m)

Atom = Tuple[str, int]      # ("btn", i) or ("sw", j)

FLS: Formula = ("fls",)


def atom(kind: str, index: int) -> Formula:
    return ("atom", (kind, index))


def imp(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("imp", p, q)


def neg(p: Formula) -> Formula:

def disj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    return imp(neg(p), q)


def top_mask(m: int) -> int:
    """⊤ = the whole space of generic objects, as a bitmask of width 2^m."""
    return (1 << (1 << m)) - 1


def generic_objects(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """The 2^m switch settings, in the order used for bit positions."""
    return [tuple(reversed(bits)) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def generic_index(g: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Bit position of the generic object g."""
    return sum(bit << k for k, bit in enumerate(g))


def make_assignment(stage: FrozenSet[int], n: int, m: int) -> Dict[Atom, int]:
    """
    Stage-`stage` assignment: a pushed button gets ⊤, an unpushed one ⊥, and
    switch j gets the set of generic objects that turn it on.
    """
    full = top_mask(m)
    assign: Dict[Atom, int] = {("btn", i): (full if i in stage else 0)
                               for i in range(n)}
    for j in range(m):
        mask = 0
        for idx, g in enumerate(generic_objects(m)):
            if g[j] == 1:
                mask |= 1 << idx
        assign[("sw", j)] = mask
    return assign


def bval(p: Formula, assign: Dict[Atom, int], m: int) -> int:
    """Boolean value ⟦p⟧ of p under the given assignment."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return 0
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return assign[p[1]]
    a = bval(p[1], assign, m)
    b = bval(p[2], assign, m)
    return (top_mask(m) & ~a) | b          # a ⇒ b  =  aᶜ ∨ b


def csat(stage: FrozenSet[int], g: Sequence[int], p: Formula) -> bool:
    """Two-valued truth of p at the control world (stage, g)."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return False
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return (i in stage) if kind == "btn" else (g[i] == 1)
    return (not csat(stage, g, p[1])) or csat(stage, g, p[2])


def realization_holds(p: Formula, stage: FrozenSet[int], n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """Verify  (S,g) ⊨ p  ⟺  g ∈ ⟦p⟧_S  for every generic object g."""
    value = bval(p, make_assignment(stage, n, m), m)
    return all(
        csat(stage, g, p) == bool(value >> generic_index(g) & 1)
        for g in generic_objects(m)
    )

World = Tuple[FrozenSet[int], Tuple[int, ...]]
Pred = Callable[[World], bool]


def worlds(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    stages = [frozenset(c) for r in range(n + 1) for c in combinations(range(n), r)]

    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))

    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))

    """Ground possibility: 'true in some universe of which this is an extension'."""
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def predicates(ws: List[World]) -> Iterator[Pred]:
    """All 2^|W| predicates on the frame."""
    index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(ws)}
    for mask in range(1 << len(ws)):

    """Exhaustive test: does the truth value depend only on the switch setting?"""
    for g in settings(m):

    nf = button_free_normal_form(p)

    return (1 << (1 << m)) - 1

    full = top_mask(m)

FLS: Formula = ("fls",)

def atom(kind: str, index: int) -> Formula:

    return ("imp", p, q)

    return imp(p, FLS)

    return neg(imp(p, neg(q)))


def disj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    return imp(neg(p), q)


def generics(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    return [tuple(reversed(b)) for b in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def csat(S: FrozenSet[int], g: Sequence[int], p: Formula) -> bool:
    if p[0] == "fls":

    if p[0] == "atom":

        return (i in S) if kind == "btn" else (g[i] == 1)
    return (not csat(S, g, p[1])) or csat(S, g, p[2])

  function orE(){ let l=andE(); for(;;){ ws(); if(src[i]==='|'){ i++; l={t:'or',a:l,b:andE()}; } else return l; } }

*A guided tour of the Boolean-valued realization of the forcing multiverse.*

---

## 1. The question behind the machine

At the foundations of mathematics sits set theory, and the most famous question it cannot answer
is the [Continuum Hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuum_hypothesis): is there a
size of infinity strictly between the whole numbers and the real line? The standard axioms can
neither prove nor refute it, and the technique that established this —
[forcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forcing_(mathematics)) — does something remarkable. It
manufactures, from one universe of sets, a *larger* one in which a chosen statement becomes true.

Forcing can be iterated. From any universe you may force, and force again. What emerges is not a
single mathematical reality but a network of them: the **set-theoretic multiverse**. And once
you have a network, a new question appears — not "is this true?" but "is this true *no matter
where you go*?"

Write $\Box p$ for "$p$ holds in every forcing extension" and $\Diamond p$ for "$p$ holds in some
forcing extension". The **modal logic of forcing** asks which combinations of these operators are
universally valid.

<details>
<summary><b>Why modal logic, of all things?</b> (click to expand)</summary>

Because forcing behaves exactly like an accessibility relation between possible worlds. The
trivial forcing changes nothing, so every universe is accessible from itself (reflexivity). An
iteration of forcings is again a forcing, so accessibility is transitive. And any two forcing
extensions of a universe can be amalgamated into a common further extension, by forcing with the
product of the two notions of forcing — a property called *directedness*. These three conditions
are precisely the frame conditions of the modal system
[$\mathsf{S4.2}$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_modal_logic).
</details>

---

## 2. The control panel

Here is the picture the entire theory turns out to be about.

Some assertions, once forced true, can never be made false again — forcing only ever *adds*
objects. Call these **buttons**: once pushed, pushed forever. Others can be forced true and then
forced false, endlessly. Call these **switches**; the Continuum Hypothesis is the canonical one.

A **world** is then a pair $(S, g)$: the finite set $S$ of buttons pushed so far, together with a
setting $g$ of all the switches. World $(S,g)$ can reach $(T,h)$ exactly when $S \subseteq T$.

Play with it. Push a button and watch a possibility disappear forever; flip a switch and watch
nothing be lost at all.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Three things are worth doing in the panel before reading on:

1. Type `~b0` (button $b_0$ is *not* pushed) at the mantle, note that $\Diamond p$ holds — then
   push $b_0$ and watch $\Box\Diamond p$ collapse. **That is the death of the axiom $5$.**
2. Type `s0` and confirm it is flagged a *switch* — both $\Diamond \mathrm{CH}$ and
   $\Diamond \neg\mathrm{CH}$ hold at every single world.
3. Type `b0 & s0` and then `s0 -> s1`, and compare the *invariant* flag. Only the second is
   invariant, because only it never mentions a button.

## 3. The frame, drawn

Rows are stages: how many buttons have been pushed. The order climbs and never descends. Every
pair of worlds has a common world above it — that is directedness — and both colours occur above
every world, which is exactly the statement that the Continuum Hypothesis is a switch.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>The formal frame laws</b></summary>

**Reflexivity.** $S \subseteq S$.

**Transitivity.** $S \subseteq T \subseteq U$ gives $S \subseteq U$.

**Directedness.** Given $(S_1,g_1)$ and $(S_2,g_2)$, the world $(S_1 \cup S_2, g_1)$ is above
both. Note this is *unconditional*: any two worlds have an upper bound.

These three yield the axioms $T$ ($\Box p \to p$), $4$ ($\Box p \to \Box\Box p$) and $.2$
($\Diamond\Box p \to \Box\Diamond p$) respectively — the system $\mathsf{S4.2}$.
</details>

---

## 4. From picture to construction: Boolean values

So far this is a nice picture. A picture is not a theorem. The real question is whether one can
*build* a mathematical structure in which all of these laws hold as consequences rather than
stipulations. The tool is
[Boolean-valued models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean-valued_model), the algebraic face of
forcing.

Instead of asking whether a statement is true or false, assign it a value $\llbracket p
\rrbracket$ in a Boolean algebra of "degrees of truth":

$$\llbracket \bot \rrbracket = \bot, \qquad \llbracket p \to q \rrbracket = \llbracket p
\rrbracket \Rightarrow \llbracket q \rrbracket, \qquad a \Rightarrow b := a^{\complement} \vee b.$$

Two theorems make this a genuine semantics for forcing.

> **Forcing Closure.** Every theorem of classical propositional logic receives value $\top$, in
> every Boolean-valued universe.

> **Truth Lemma.** Choose a **generic filter** $U$ — a set of Boolean values containing $\top$,
> omitting $\bot$, closed upward and under meets, and *deciding* every element in the sense that
> $a \in U$ or $a^{\complement} \in U$. Collapse the universe by declaring an atom true exactly
> when its value lies in $U$. Then for *every* assertion, $p$ is true in this **generic quotient**
> iff $\llbracket p \rrbracket \in U$.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketches</b></summary>

*Forcing closure* is an induction on Hilbert-style derivations. It suffices that the three axiom
schemes become Boolean identities — each provable by the residuation law
$c \le a \Rightarrow b \iff c \wedge a \le b$ — and that modus ponens is sound, which follows
from $a \wedge (a \Rightarrow b) \le b$.

*The truth lemma* is an induction on formulas. The only content is that a generic filter respects
Boolean implication: $a \Rightarrow b \in U$ iff ($a \in U$ implies $b \in U$). Left to right uses
$a \wedge (a\Rightarrow b) \le b$; right to left splits on whether $a \in U$, using decisiveness
in the negative case.
</details>

The algorithm below is the truth lemma made executable: Boolean values as bitmasks over the space
of generic objects.

## 5. Independence, for free

Here is the payoff of the algebraic view. Suppose an assertion has a value that is *neither*
$\bot$ nor $\top$, and suppose the algebra is **rich**: every nonzero element belongs to some
generic filter. (For a powerset algebra this is free — take the principal filter at any point.)

> **Branching Theorem.** If $\llbracket p \rrbracket \notin \{\bot, \top\}$, there are two generic
> filters whose quotients disagree about $p$: one satisfies it, the other refutes it.

Independence is no longer two separate constructions. It is the shadow of a single element of a
Boolean algebra failing to be $0$ or $1$.

The heat map below makes this visible. Each row is an assertion; each column a generic object; a
filled cell means the corresponding world satisfies the assertion. Uniform rows are decided;
mixed rows *are* the branches of the multiverse.

{{visualization:2}}

---

## 6. The realization: the panel *is* a Boolean-valued universe

Now close the loop. Take the Boolean algebra to be the powerset of the space $\mathcal{G}$ of
switch settings. At stage $S$, a pushed button gets value $\mathcal{G}$, an unpushed one
$\varnothing$, and switch $s$ gets $\{ g : g(s) = 1\}$.

> **Realization Theorem.** For every stage $S$, every generic object $g$ and every assertion $p$,
> $$(S,g) \models p \iff g \in \llbracket p \rrbracket_S .$$

The hand-drawn world $(S,g)$ *is* the generic quotient of the stage-$S$ Boolean-valued universe by
the principal generic filter at $g$. And now the frame laws stop being assumptions:

- **Buttons are derived.** Assertions built from button atoms by $\wedge$ and $\vee$ have Boolean
  values monotone in the stage, so by the realization theorem they satisfy $p \to \Box p$.
- **Both CH branches are derived.** The value of the CH switch is neither empty (the all-on
  generic object is in it) nor everything (the all-off one is not), so the Branching Theorem
  applies verbatim.
- **Directedness is derived** from the union of stages, which on the algebra side is the join of
  Boolean values.

<details>
<summary><b>Why this matters: the falsifiable obligation</b></summary>

An abstract theory may simply *postulate* that the multiverse frame is directed and carries
buttons and switches. The realization theorem discharges the corresponding obligation: there is
*one* satisfaction relation, arising from an honest construction, for which reflexivity,
transitivity, directedness, the button law, the switch law and both branch conditions all hold
simultaneously. Had any one of them failed, the construction would have refuted the abstract
frame.
</details>

---

## 7. Exactly $\mathsf{S4.2}$ — no more, no less

The logic is pinned down from both sides.

- **$.2$ is exactly directedness.** If the schema $\Diamond \Box p \to \Box \Diamond p$ holds for
  *every* predicate, then the frame must be directed. (Apply it to the predicate "$y$ can reach
  me".)
- **The frame validates $5$ if and only if there are no buttons.** One button suffices to kill
  $\mathsf{S5}$: let $p$ say "$b$ is unpushed"; at the mantle $\Diamond p$ holds, but after
  pushing $b$ it never can again.
- **Two independent buttons refute linearity $.3$.** Push $b_1$ alone and $b_2$ alone: neither
  disjunct of $\Box(\Box p \to q) \vee \Box(\Box q \to p)$ survives. The multiverse genuinely
  branches; it is not a chain.

Because a Hilbert calculus for $\mathsf{S4.2}$ can be proved sound on *every* directed preorder,
each of these finite refutations doubles as an **independence proof**: neither $5$ nor $.3$ is a
theorem of $\mathsf{S4.2}$.

The checker below verifies all of this by brute force over every predicate on a finite frame.

## 8. What is true *everywhere*?

A multiverse invites a notion of truth stronger than "true here". Which assertions never change
value as you move around?

> **Invariant Fragment Theorem.** An assertion has the same truth value at all worlds sharing a
> switch setting — i.e. it is preserved by forcing extensions *and* by passing back down to
> grounds — **iff** it is equivalent to a **button-free** assertion, one built from switch atoms
> alone.

<details>
<summary><b>The proof, in one move</b></summary>

Given an invariant $p$, substitute $\bot$ for every button atom. The result $p^{\bot}$ is
button-free by construction, and an induction shows it computes the truth value of $p$ at the
empty stage. Invariance transfers that value to every stage, so $p$ and $p^{\bot}$ agree
everywhere. Sharpness is immediate: a bare button atom changes value when the button is pushed,
so it is not invariant.
</details>

The lesson generalizes: preservation *upward* alone gives necessity above a world, not truth
throughout the multiverse. Genuine invariance is **bidirectional**. That motivates a second
modality $\check{\Diamond}$, reading "in some *ground*" — some universe of which this one is a
forcing extension. On the very same frame:

$$p \to \Box\,\check{\Diamond}\,p \quad \text{is valid}, \qquad\text{while}\qquad p \to \Box \Diamond p \quad\text{fails}.$$

So the two-way logic of the multiverse is strictly richer than the one-way logic of forcing. (You
can test both lines live in the control panel above.)

{{algorithm:3}}

---

## 9. Counting the panel

A last, concrete fact with a pretty proof.

> With $n$ buttons and $m$ switches, the frame has $2^{n+m}$ worlds and exactly $3^n \cdot 4^m$
> accessible pairs.

Each button contributes three states to an accessible pair $(w,v)$: unpushed in both, pushed in
$v$ only, pushed in both. The fourth combination — pushed in $w$ but not in $v$ — is exactly what
the no-undo rule forbids. Each switch contributes four, since its value before and after is
unconstrained. The identity behind it is $\sum_{t \subseteq s} 2^{|t|} = 3^{|s|}$.

{{visualization:1}}

{{algorithm:1}}

forcing closure, the truth lemma, the realization theorem, the frame laws and the failures of
$5$, $\mathrm{B}$ and $.3$, derived buttons, derived CH branches, the invariant fragment theorem,

## Where this leaves us

None of this decides the Continuum Hypothesis; it was never going to. What it does is change the
register of the question. Instead of asking which statements are true, we get a precise account
of how truth *moves*: which assertions lock in, which oscillate forever, which are invisible to
the motion, and exactly which laws of necessity and possibility that motion obeys.

And the account is not a picture with a story attached. The control panel of irreversible buttons
and free switches is a generic quotient of a Boolean-valued universe — a forcing construction, in
disguise.

import Logic.Multiverse.InvariantFragment

namespace S42Independence

open BooleanValuedRealization MultiverseInvariantFragment

/-! ## The modal language and its Kripke semantics -/

/-- Modal formulas over propositional atoms `α`. -/
inductive MForm (α : Type*) where
  | atom : α → MForm α
  | fls : MForm α
  | imp : MForm α → MForm α → MForm α
  | box : MForm α → MForm α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace MForm
variable {α : Type*}

/-- Negation. -/
def neg (p : MForm α) : MForm α := .imp p .fls
/-- Disjunction. -/
def disj (p q : MForm α) : MForm α := .imp (neg p) q
/-- Possibility. -/
def dia (p : MForm α) : MForm α := neg (.box (neg p))

end MForm

variable {α W : Type*}

/-- Kripke satisfaction. -/
def msat (R : W → W → Prop) (V : α → W → Prop) : MForm α → W → Prop
  | .atom a => V a
  | .fls => fun _ => False
  | .imp p q => fun w => msat R V p w → msat R V q w
  | .box p => fun w => ∀ v, R w v → msat R V p v

/-- Derivability in `S4.2`: classical propositional logic (`ax1`–`ax3`) with the

inductive S42 {α : Type*} : MForm α → Prop
  | ax1 (p q : MForm α) : S42 (.imp p (.imp q p))
  | ax2 (p q r : MForm α) :
      S42 (.imp (.imp p (.imp q r)) (.imp (.imp p q) (.imp p r)))
  | ax3 (p : MForm α) : S42 (.imp (MForm.neg (MForm.neg p)) p)
  | axK (p q : MForm α) :
      S42 (.imp (.box (.imp p q)) (.imp (.box p) (.box q)))
  | axT (p : MForm α) : S42 (.imp (.box p) p)
  | ax4 (p : MForm α) : S42 (.imp (.box p) (.box (.box p)))
  | axDot2 (p : MForm α) : S42 (.imp (MForm.dia (.box p)) (.box (MForm.dia p)))
  | mp {p q : MForm α} : S42 (.imp p q) → S42 p → S42 q
  | nec {p : MForm α} : S42 p → S42 (.box p)

/-- A **directed preorder**: the abstract shape of a forcing frame. -/
structure DirectedPreorder (W : Type*) where
  /-- The accessibility relation. -/
  rel : W → W → Prop
  refl : ∀ w, rel w w
  trans : ∀ {w v u}, rel w v → rel v u → rel w u
  dir : ∀ x y z, rel x y → rel x z → ∃ u, rel y u ∧ rel z u

theorem S42_sound (F : DirectedPreorder W) {p : MForm α} (h : S42 p) :

  induction h with

  | ax2 p q r => intro V w; simp only [msat_imp]; tauto
  | ax3 p => intro V w; simp only [msat_imp, msat_neg]; tauto
  | axK p q => intro V w hpq hp v hv; exact hpq v hv (hp v hv)
  | axT p => intro V w hp; exact hp w (F.refl w)
  | ax4 p => intro V w hp v hwv u hvu; exact hp u (F.trans hwv hvu)
  | axDot2 p =>
      intro V w hdia v hwv
      rw [msat_dia] at hdia
      obtain ⟨t, hwt, hbox⟩ := hdia
      obtain ⟨u, htu, hvu⟩ := F.dir w t v hwt hwv
      rw [msat_dia]
      exact ⟨u, hvu, hbox u htu⟩
  | mp _ _ ih1 ih2 => intro V w; exact ih1 V w (ih2 V w)
  | nec _ ih => intro V w v _; exact ih V v

/-- The two-button, one-switch forcing frame, packaged as a directed preorder. -/
def ctrlFrame : DirectedPreorder (CWorld Bool Unit) where

  dir := fun _ y z _ _ =>

theorem compl_mem_iff (a : B) : U.mem aᶜ ↔ ¬ U.mem a := by

/-- Two-valued satisfaction of an assertion at a two-valued world. -/
def sat (w : α → Prop) : BForm α → Prop
  | .atom a => w a
  | .fls => False
  | .imp p q => sat w p → sat w q

@[simp] theorem sat_atom (w : α → Prop) (a : α) : sat w (.atom a) ↔ w a := Iff.rfl
@[simp] theorem sat_fls (w : α → Prop) : ¬ sat w (.fls : BForm α) := id
@[simp] theorem sat_imp (w : α → Prop) (p q : BForm α) :
    sat w (.imp p q) ↔ (sat w p → sat w q) := Iff.rfl
@[simp] theorem sat_neg (w : α → Prop) (p : BForm α) :
    sat w p.neg ↔ ¬ sat w p := Iff.rfl
@[simp] theorem sat_tru (w : α → Prop) : sat w (BForm.tru : BForm α) := id

@[simp] theorem sat_conj (w : α → Prop) (p q : BForm α) :
    sat w (p.conj q) ↔ sat w p ∧ sat w q := by
  simp only [BForm.conj, sat_neg, sat_imp]
  tauto

@[simp] theorem sat_disj (w : α → Prop) (p q : BForm α) :
    sat w (p.disj q) ↔ sat w p ∨ sat w q := by
  simp only [BForm.disj, sat_imp, sat_neg]
  tauto

/-- Satisfaction depends only on the atomic truth values. -/
theorem sat_congr {w w' : α → Prop} (h : ∀ a, w a ↔ w' a) (p : BForm α) :
    sat w p ↔ sat w' p := by
  induction p with
  | atom a => exact h a
  | fls => rfl
  | imp p q ihp ihq => simp [ihp, ihq]
